title: When and What to Teach: Budget-Aware Online Adaptation for Web Agents

paper.title: When and What to Teach: Budget-Aware Online Adaptation for Web Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Web agents have achieved significant success in automating complex internet tasks but deploying them in real-world environments requires continuous online adaptation. Given that deploying powerful proprietary models remains commercially cost-prohibitive, practitioners must rely on lightweight local models that evolve post-deployment via online teaching from a stronger teacher. However, standard interactive feedback imposes prohibitive costs. We show that conventional trajectory-level preference optimization wastes budget on both unresolvable episodes and redundant execution turns. To resolve these inefficiencies, we propose Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming , a budget-aware framework that systematically orchestrates when and what to teach. Specifically, our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to dictate when to query the teacher model and a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide what informative turns to retain. Extensive experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp demonstrate that our method achieves comparable first-pass success while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjw131f1fc/budgeted-online-teaching .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Web agents Wang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026c) ; Wei et al. (2025) ; Krupp et al. (2025) are autonomous software entities designed to navigate the internet and execute complex digital workflows by perceiving webpage environments and executing concrete browser actions such as clicking, typing, or scrolling. By coupling LLM-based web reasoning with sequential browser interactions, these systems have demonstrated significant promise in automating real-world internet tasks Nakano et al. (2021) ; Yao et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) . However, static offline training often fails to generalize when agents are deployed in real interactive environments characterized by evolving user interfaces, stochastic network behaviors, and unseen workflows Zhou et al. (2024) ; Deng et al. (2023) ; Xie et al. (2024) ; Koh et al. (2024) . Meanwhile, directly deploying powerful proprietary models for every task remains commercially cost-prohibitive, so practitioners rely on lightweight local models that must adapt and evolve post-deployment. A natural solution to mitigate these deployment-phase errors is online teaching. Under this paradigm, whenever the student encounters an execution failure, the teacher is queried to produce a corrective demonstration, thereby updating the student before the next streaming task arrives Hinton et al. (2015) . Unlike standard online reinforcement learning, where the agent explores freely, here the agent is already deployed and first-pass success matters on every episode. This deployment-time online adaptation setting remains, to our knowledge, under-explored for web agents. The most intuitive implementation to realize this workflow is to pair every student failure with a full teacher trajectory and directly feed both elements into a trajectory-level preference optimization objective such as DPO Rafailov et al. (2024) . Nevertheless, we argue that such an unselective, full-trajectory strategy inherently suffers from inefficient supervision allocation, treating expert supervision as an infinite commodity rather than a strictly bottlenecked, strategic resource. This inefficiency manifests acutely at two distinct granularities, corresponding to the critical yet fundamentally overlooked dimensions of when and what to teach. At the episode level ( when ), the baseline treats all student failures as equally worth querying, ignoring that the teacher itself is unstable on many tasks and will fail to produce a usable corrective trajectory, wasting the query budget without return Zhang and Cho (2016) ; Hoque et al. (2022) . At the trajectory level ( what ), it indiscriminately trains on the entire action history, overlooking that long-horizon web sequences are typically riddled with redundant navigation pauses and non-essential actions Belkhale et al. (2023) . Striking a budget-aware balance across both axes simultaneously remains an open and critical challenge. To address this issue, we present Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming , a budget-aware online adaptation framework that systematically orchestrates when and what to teach. Our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to determine when to query the teacher model. Tactically, we devise a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide what to teach by retaining the most informative turns on both sides. Crucially, both components are fully compatible with various preference optimization objectives, allowing our framework to be seamlessly applied to standard criteria such as DPO Rafailov et al. (2024) and SimPO Meng et al. (2024) . Experiments on MiniWoB Liu et al. (2018) and TimeWarp Ishmam and Marino (2026) show that our method achieves comparable online first-pass success to the full-trajectory baselines while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. The contributions of this paper are: ∙ \bullet We formulate online web-agent teaching as a budget allocation problem along two axes: when to query the teacher and what turns to retain for training. ∙ \bullet We introduce a solvability-aware teacher gate that reduces unnecessary teacher queries based on historical teacher outcomes. ∙ \bullet We introduce a score-guided turn selection that reduces redundant training tokens based on the student’s current log-probability. ∙ \bullet Experiments on two online web-agent benchmarks validate the framework, showing comparable first-pass success with substantially reduced teacher-query and student-training costs.

sections.heading: 2.1 Web Agents and Online Adaptation
sections.text: Online adaptation for web agents differs from standard online reinforcement learning, where the agent explores freely to maximize long-term reward. In our setting the agent is already deployed, first-pass success matters on every episode, and teacher supervision carries real cost. Early web-agent work such as WebGPT Nakano et al. (2021) and WebShop Yao et al. (2022) learns primarily from successful demonstrations. LEAP Choudhury and Sodhi (2025) introduces iterative fine-tuning from privileged AI feedback on student failures, but assumes unrestricted teacher access and optimizes for final model quality rather than first-pass success on each episode as it arrives. Other approaches improve agents through inference-time experience reuse without gradient updates Shinn et al. (2023) ; Zhao et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2023) . On the training side, DPO Rafailov et al. (2024) replaces explicit reward modeling Christiano et al. (2017) ; Schulman et al. (2017) with direct preference optimization, and recent work extends it to trajectory-level, segment-level, or step-level agent objectives Shi et al. (2024) ; Kong et al. (2025) ; Lai et al. (2024) ; Xiong et al. (2024) ; Song et al. (2024) ; Cao et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026b) . These methods focus on how to construct the preference loss from a given trajectory pool. We instead study which trajectories to collect and which turns to retain under budget constraints.

sections.heading: 2.2 Active and Budget-Aware Imitation
sections.text: Selectively requesting expert supervision originates from active learning Settles (2009) and active imitation learning, where learners query costly expert interventions only on informative states. DAgger Ross et al. (2011) iteratively queries expert actions on learner-visited states to mitigate compounding errors, but it assumes unrestricted expert access. Subsequent variations reduce this cost by gating queries on safety or novelty signals. For instance, SafeDAgger Zhang and Cho (2016) queries only on predicted deviations, ThriftyDAgger Hoque et al. (2022) targets an explicit intervention budget, and HG-DAgger Kelly et al. (2019) allows human-gated interventions in embodied control. These methods decide whether to query at the level of individual states using local uncertainty signals. In contrast, our teacher gate estimates whether the current failure is teacher-solvable based on historical outcomes. Furthermore, none of these methods address what to retain once a demonstration is collected. While prior work on demonstration quality Belkhale et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2026a) filters entire episodes, we focus on a finer turn-level selection mechanism.

sections.heading: 2.3 Difficulty-Aware Data Selection for Preference Learning
sections.text: A separate line of work uses the current model’s own scores as a signal for selecting or weighting training data. Perplexity- and log-probability-based filtering has been used to curate pretraining and fine-tuning corpora by retaining examples the model finds informative Ankner et al. (2025) ; Xie et al. (2023) ; Marion et al. (2023) , and hard-example mining and curriculum strategies have long been used to focus training on instances the current model gets wrong Shrivastava et al. (2016) ; Bengio et al. (2009) . In preference learning, recent work moves from full-response DPO toward finer-grained credit assignment, including step-level Lai et al. (2024) ; Xiong et al. (2024) , segment-level Kong et al. (2025) , and token-level Zeng et al. (2024) objectives that re-weight or restrict the contrastive signal to portions of the response. These approaches share the high-level intuition of concentrating supervision on informative portions, but they typically apply a single criterion uniformly and operate at sub-action granularity. Our turn-level selection differs by operating at the interaction-turn level and applying a dual criterion: hardest turns on the positive side, most-likely-to-repeat turns on the negative side.

sections.text: We consider a fixed-order online task stream { x t } t = 1 T \{x_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} Shalev-Shwartz (2025) , where each task x t x_{t} corresponds to a web navigation goal. The student policy π θ \pi_{\theta} processes tasks sequentially in a first-pass manner: at episode t t , the student executes independently and produces trajectory τ t S = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s L , a L ) \tau_{t}^{S}=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{L},a_{L}) , where s i s_{i} denotes the page state and a i a_{i} the student action. sections.heading: 3.2 Method Overview
sections.text: We find that straightforwardly querying the teacher after every student failure and optimizing full trajectories indiscriminately wastes budget at both the episode and turn levels. This inefficiency arises because some failures are inherently unresolvable for the teacher, while even successful rollouts contain redundant, task-specific details with minimal learning value. To resolve these inefficiencies, we organize online teaching into a two-stage mechanism as illustrated in Figure 1 . The solvability-aware teacher gate first operates at the episode level to decide whether a student failure warrants an expert rollout. Subsequently, the score-guided turn selection mechanism functions at the turn level to filter the most informative turns from both the positive and negative trajectories, assembling a trimmed preference pair. This optimized pair is then utilized to update the student via a trajectory-level preference optimization objective. sections.heading: 3.3 Solvability-Aware Teacher Query Gating
sections.text: The value of a teacher query depends on whether the current failure can be converted into an effective teaching package: if the teacher is also unstable on the current task, querying it only consumes budget without producing a usable matched positive trajectory. To address this, we maintain an episode-level teacher memory ℳ \mathcal{M} that records teacher outcomes on historical failures. Each failure is keyed by a semantic task representation ϕ ⁡ ( x i ) ∈ ℝ d \phi(x_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that encodes the task name and goal description, and ℳ \mathcal{M} stores entries { ( ϕ ⁡ ( x i ) , y i ) } \{(\phi(x_{i}),\ y_{i})\} , where y i = 1 y_{i}=1 if the corresponding teacher rollout produced an accepted matched-positive package and y i = 0 y_{i}=0 otherwise. The teacher gate thus concentrates the limited teacher-query budget on failures more likely to yield effective teaching packages, while keeping the memory adaptive to drift in the failure distribution.

Under a fixed budget of at most M M turns per side, the goal is to identify the most informative local sub-trajectories from both sequences. On the positive side , we retain the turns that the current student finds most difficult, as lower student log-probabilities indicate higher incremental learning value Mindermann et al. (2022) . While negative-side scores are obtained for free from the student rollout, positive-side scoring requires one additional student forward pass. This selection process thus concentrates the training budget on the local segments least familiar to the current student.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: Online teaching is fundamentally a streaming setting: the student receives tasks one by one and must adapt as the stream unfolds. We therefore organize each benchmark into a fixed-order online task stream and use that stream as a controlled evaluation protocol shared across all methods. MiniWoB ( Liu et al., 2018 ) is instantiated as a 125-episode stream covering form filling, email operations, search, and other common web interaction patterns. TimeWarp ( Ishmam and Marino, 2026 ) is instantiated as a 150-episode stream with longer and more heterogeneous tasks, placing greater demands on cross-task generalization. The task ordering is completely fixed offline and reused for every method, so that any difference in observed performance reflects the online learning behavior rather than variation in the task sequence, and all methods report first-pass results on the same evaluation stream of tasks.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Baseline Student applies no online teaching and reflects the student’s initial capability. Teacher Baseline runs the teacher independently on the same task stream, providing an upper-bound reference. Among online teaching methods, Naive SFT fine-tunes on matched teacher-positive trajectories without using student failure trajectories as negative signal. We then consider two trajectory-level preference optimization carriers, applied directly between complete teacher-positive and student-failed trajectories with no selection mechanism: Trajectory DPO and Trajectory SimPO . On top of each carrier, + Query Gate adds episode-level teacher query gating, and + Query Gate + Turn Selection (our full method) further adds score-guided turn-level trimming.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: The primary metric is online first-pass success (number of episodes succeeded on the first attempt). We also report %T (success as a percentage of teacher success) and Upd. (number of student updates triggered during the stream). Budget metrics include teacher calls, failed positive resolutions (teacher calls that fail to produce an acceptable matched-positive trajectory), and Student Total PFLOPs (training plus positive-side scoring overhead). PFLOPs are computed under a dense-equivalent assumption from replay-counted tokens. Full accounting is in Appendix D .

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: The student model is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct Yang et al. (2025) and the teacher is GPT-4o Hurst et al. (2024) . All rollouts use the standard GenericAgent from AgentLab on top of the BrowserGym ecosystem Chezelles et al. (2025) . Teacher and student share the same observation and action configuration and differ only in the chat-model backend (OpenAI API vs. a local vLLM Kwon et al. (2023) endpoint). All methods use LoRA Hu et al. (2022) ; Dettmers et al. (2023) fine-tuning. DPO uses Eq. 3 with β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 , and SimPO uses Eq. 4 with β = 2.0 \beta=2.0 and γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 . Gate thresholds λ \lambda / ε exp \varepsilon_{\rm exp} are 0.35 0.35 / 0.50 0.50 on MiniWoB and 0.30 0.30 / 0.50 0.50 on TimeWarp. Turn budgets are top- 3 3 /side for MiniWoB and top- 4 4 /side for TimeWarp. Full hyperparameters, optimizer settings, and agent and gate configuration details are detailed in Appendix A and Appendix B .

sections.heading: 4.4 Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: Inspecting individual teaching packages clarifies what score-guided turn selection actually keeps and discards, and the retained turns consistently track the student’s current weakness across both benchmarks, which a positional heuristic such as keeping the most recent turns cannot reproduce. Full trimmed pairs with per-turn scores are given in Appendix C . A representative MiniWoB case is use-autocomplete , where the goal is to enter an item beginning with “Gua” and ending with “uam”. The teacher types the prefix to trigger the autocomplete dropdown, picks the suggestion Guam , edits it into Guaguam , and submits. Score-guided selection retains the autocomplete-trigger and the subsequent text edit while dropping the trailing submit, which the student already handles. The matching student-failure trajectory submits the prefix prematurely, retries, and eventually enters the malformed word Guamau . The selector retains exactly these turns, capturing the failure mode the student is most likely to repeat. The trimmed pair thus concentrates the imitation signal on the corrective subroutine and the contrastive signal on the recurring error. The same behavior carries over to longer TimeWarp tasks. On a multi-hop search task that requires opening the fourth result for “Utah”, identifying “New Orleans” as the first city in the article, searching for it, and reporting the final state name from its fourth result, the teacher’s complete trajectory contains routine search-box fills and Go clicks. Selection drops the initial search-box fill and both routine Go clicks, while retaining the two cross-article jumps, the intermediate New Orleans query, and the final answer, which together form the actual reasoning chain the student must learn. The matching student trajectory never reaches this chain: it diverts into the Sci/Tech section and opens an unrelated technology article, and the negative side preserves exactly this divergence while dropping the closing “incomplete task” message.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we investigated online teaching for web agents under realistic budget constraints. Driven by the fact that deploying proprietary models is commercially cost-prohibitive, we enabled lightweight local models to effectively adapt and evolve post-deployment. To eliminate the inefficiencies of unresolvable queries and redundant execution turns in full-trajectory optimization, we realized a two-stage budget allocation framework. Specifically, our method integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate using a k-NN historical memory to filter queries alongside a score-guided turn selection mechanism to retain only highly informative execution segments. This joint formulation allows the student model to systematically establish a clear understanding of when to seek external assistance and what critical behaviors to replicate. Experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp show that our framework achieves comparable or superior online success compared to trajectory-level DPO while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. These substantial gains establish a highly cost-effective paradigm for future scalable online intelligence.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our evaluation focuses on simulated web-agent benchmarks. Extending the framework to live websites, multi-modal computer-use tasks, or non-English interfaces is a natural next step but does not require architectural changes. The teacher gate uses a standard text-embedding model for k k -NN retrieval; while this worked well in our setting, environments with highly heterogeneous page structures may benefit from domain-adapted embeddings. The current turn selection criterion is based solely on the student’s log-probability. Incorporating additional signals such as state novelty or action diversity could further refine the selection, though our ablations suggest the current criterion already captures the dominant source of variation. Finally, our framework assumes a single fixed teacher model. Exploring multi-teacher or self-improving teacher configurations is an interesting direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Agent and Prompt Configuration
sections.text: All rollouts use the standard GenericAgent class from AgentLab on top of BrowserGym Chezelles et al. (2025) with the default FLAGS_GPT_4o preset. We did not modify the AgentLab prompt template or action parser. The contributions of this paper are in the teacher query gate, turn scoring and selection, and the student update logic, not in hand-engineered web-agent prompts. Teacher and student agents share the same observation, action, and prompt configuration and differ only in the chat-model backend: the teacher uses the OpenAI API (GPT-4o), and the student uses a local vLLM endpoint serving Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, with rollout log-probability access exposed by the inference wrapper.

sections.heading: Observation.
sections.text: The agent observes the page through the AXTree representation provided by BrowserGym, augmented with the currently focused element, the recent interaction history, the recent action history, and current error logs. Visible and clickable tags are preserved in the AXTree. HTML dumps, screenshots, set-of-mark annotations, coordinate extraction, and historical thoughts are disabled. Concretely, the relevant FLAGS_GPT_4o.obs fields are set as: use_ax_tree=True , use_html=False , use_screenshot=False , use_som=False , use_focused_element=True , use_history=True , use_action_history=True , use_think_history=False , use_error_logs=True , extract_visible_tag=True , extract_clickable_tag=True , extract_coords=False .

sections.heading: Action Space.
sections.text: We use the standard bid-based high-level action set from BrowserGym ( action_set.subsets=("bid",) ), restricted to single-action steps ( multiaction=False ). The exact set of available actions depends on the environment: MiniWoB tasks typically expose click , fill , and keyboard_press . TimeWarp additionally exposes navigation actions such as go_back , goto , tab_focus , and send_msg_to_user . Action descriptions are kept in their default short form ( long_description=False , individual_examples=False ).

sections.heading: Prompt Switches.
sections.text: We use the default FLAGS_GPT_4o prompt switches: use_thinking=True , use_abstract_example=True , use_concrete_example=True , use_hints=True , use_plan=False , use_memory=False , use_criticise=False , enable_chat=False . The prompt token budget is max_prompt_tokens=40000 with up to max_trunc_itr=20 truncation iterations when the budget is exceeded.

sections.heading: Appendix B Full Hyperparameter and Gate Configuration
sections.text: This appendix lists training, optimizer, and gate configuration details that are condensed in Section 4 (Implementation details).

sections.heading: LoRA and Training Objectives.
sections.text: All methods fine-tune the student with LoRA (rank = 16 =16 , scaling = 32 =32 , dropout = 0.05 =0.05 ) on q_proj , k_proj , v_proj , o_proj , gate_proj , up_proj , and down_proj . Naive SFT applies only an SFT update to an available positive teaching trajectory. DPO uses the standard objective in Eq. 3 with β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 and an explicit reference model; the reference is the current stable student state for each update, with the clean base model used for the first update. SimPO uses the reference-free objective in Eq. 4 with β = 2.0 \beta=2.0 and γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 . DPO and SimPO use no SFT preheat, auxiliary SFT loss, or anchor SFT examples. After every successful update, the promoted student state is used for the next episode.

sections.heading: Optimizer.
sections.text: We use AdamW with learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} on MiniWoB and 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} on TimeWarp, warmup ratio 0.05 0.05 , effective batch size 8 8 , and 1 1 epoch per online update. Maximum sequence lengths are 4,000 tokens for MiniWoB and 7,000 tokens for TimeWarp.

sections.heading: Teacher Gate.
sections.text: The teacher memory retrieves k = 10 k=10 neighbors with similarity bandwidth κ = 0.16 \kappa=0.16 . The solvability threshold λ \lambda and exploration evidence threshold ε exp \varepsilon_{\rm exp} are 0.35 0.35 / 0.50 0.50 on MiniWoB and 0.30 0.30 / 0.50 0.50 on TimeWarp. The semantic task representation ϕ ⁡ ( x ) \phi(x) is computed by encoding the string task=<task_name>; goal=<task_goal> with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small OpenAI (2024) . The embedding API is called once per gate evaluation, and its token cost is negligible compared to the teacher rollout cost and is not counted in the teacher token totals.

sections.heading: Turn Selection.
sections.text: Turn budgets are top- 3 3 /side for MiniWoB and top- 4 4 /side for TimeWarp. Negative-side scoring reuses the log-probabilities recorded during the student’s own rollout and incurs no additional cost. Positive-side scoring requires one student forward pass per teacher-positive turn.

sections.heading: Appendix C Full Trimmed Trajectory Pairs
sections.text: This appendix complements the qualitative analysis in Section 4.4 by showing the full teacher-positive and student-failure trajectories of the two examples, together with the turns selected by score-guided turn selection on each side. The reported selection score is the per-side criterion from Section 3.4 , normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] within the trajectory: on the positive side it ranks turns by lowest student log-probability (turns the student finds most difficult), and on the negative side it ranks turns by highest student log-probability (failure turns the student is most likely to repeat). Selected turns are the top- M M turns by score on each side, where M = 3 M=3 on MiniWoB and M = 4 M=4 on TimeWarp, matching the main experimental setup.

sections.heading: Appendix D PFLOPs Accounting
sections.text: This appendix details how the Student Total PFLOPs column reported in Section 4 is computed. All numbers are derived from a single accounting pass over the exported per-update datasets, rather than from in-flight runtime estimates.

sections.heading: Dense-equivalent assumption.
sections.text: We compute student-side PFLOPs using a dense-transformer equivalent with P = 3 × 10 9 P=3\times 10^{9} parameters, matching the parameter count of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters but the forward and backward passes still involve the full dense weights, so the dense-equivalent count is the appropriate coefficient for compute reporting.

sections.heading: Training PFLOPs.
sections.text: Training cost is recomputed from the exported per-update datasets, not from runtime estimates. For each online update, we re-tokenize the dataset files with the student tokenizer under the run’s maximum sequence length. We apply method-specific coefficients reflecting the number of forward and backward passes per training token: • Naive SFT and SimPO : coefficient 6 6 (one forward + one backward pass), Train PFLOPs = 6 ⋅ P ⋅ N train 10 15 . \text{Train PFLOPs}=\frac{6\cdot P\cdot N_{\mathrm{train}}}{10^{15}}. (5) • DPO-based methods : coefficient 8 8 , because DPO requires two forward passes (policy and reference) plus one backward pass per training token, Train PFLOPs = 8 ⋅ P ⋅ N train 10 15 . \text{Train PFLOPs}=\frac{8\cdot P\cdot N_{\mathrm{train}}}{10^{15}}. (6) For methods with score-guided turn selection, the positive-side scoring forward pass (coefficient 2 2 ) is added to the objective-dependent training cost: Student Total PFLOPs = c obj ⋅ P ⋅ N train + 2 ⋅ P ⋅ N score + 10 15 , \text{Student Total PFLOPs}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{obj}}\cdot P\cdot N_{\mathrm{train}}+2\cdot P\cdot N^{+}_{\mathrm{score}}}{10^{15}}, (7) where c obj = 6 c_{\mathrm{obj}}=6 for Naive SFT and SimPO and c obj = 8 c_{\mathrm{obj}}=8 for DPO. Here, N score + N^{+}_{\mathrm{score}} is the token count of the positive-side scoring requests, read from the per-update score request log. For methods without turn selection, Student Total PFLOPs equals Train PFLOPs directly.

sections.heading: Per-update Tokens.
sections.text: Each successful online update trains only on the teaching package produced for the current episode. Previously collected teaching packages are not replayed by the main training path. The accounting pass re-tokenizes each exported per-update dataset and counts its tokens once, on the update where they contribute to the gradient.

sections.heading: Negative-side Scoring is Excluded.
sections.text: Negative-side turns are generated by the student policy itself during rollout, so the per-turn log-probabilities log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a j S ∣ s j S ) \log\pi_{\theta}(a_{j}^{S}\mid s_{j}^{S}) used by the negative-side selector are available as rollout-time inference outputs and do not require a separate forward pass.

sections.heading: Compute Budget.
sections.text: All experiments were run on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs. Each online run colocated student rollout through vLLM and LoRA fine-tuning on one GPU; for DPO, the explicit reference model was held on CPU. Multiple independent runs could execute concurrently on different GPUs. We report artifact-derived Student PFLOPs rather than an aggregate GPU-hour estimate.

All artifacts are used in a manner consistent with their intended use. We do not redistribute any of the above models or datasets.

sections.heading: Appendix F Data and Privacy
sections.text: Both benchmarks consist of synthetic or curated web-interaction tasks released by their authors for research on web agents. We use them as published, without modification, and we do not collect any new user data. The tasks do not contain personally identifying information about end users.

sections.heading: Appendix G Use of AI Assistants
sections.text: We used general-purpose LLM-based assistants to help with code drafting and writing polish (e.g., grammar and phrasing). All technical content, experimental design, and results were authored, reviewed, and verified by the authors. AI assistants were not used to generate or interpret experimental results.

sections.heading: Appendix H Potential Risks
sections.text: Our method targets web-agent adaptation in controlled benchmark environments and does not involve human subjects, harmful content generation, or deployment to live web services. As with any LLM-based agent, deploying derivatives of this work to real websites would require additional safety considerations (rate limiting, action whitelisting, error monitoring) that are out of scope for this paper.

Given that deploying powerful proprietary models remains commercially cost-prohibitive, practitioners must rely on lightweight local models that evolve post-deployment via online teaching from a stronger teacher. However, standard interactive feedback imposes prohibitive costs. We show that conventional trajectory-level preference optimization wastes budget on both unresolvable episodes and redundant execution turns. To resolve these inefficiencies, we propose Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming , a budget-aware framework that systematically orchestrates when and what to teach. Specifically, our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to dictate when to query the teacher model and a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide what informative turns to retain. Extensive experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp demonstrate that our method achieves comparable first-pass success while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjw131f1fc/budgeted-online-teaching . 2 2 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Web agents Wang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026c) ; Wei et al. (2025) ; Krupp et al. (2025) are autonomous software entities designed to navigate the internet and execute complex digital workflows by perceiving webpage environments and executing concrete browser actions such as clicking, typing, or scrolling. By coupling LLM-based web reasoning with sequential browser interactions, these systems have demonstrated significant promise in automating real-world internet tasks Nakano et al. (2021) ; Yao et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) . However, static offline training often fails to generalize when agents are deployed in real interactive environments characterized by evolving user interfaces, stochastic network behaviors, and unseen workflows Zhou et al. (2024) ; Deng et al. (2023) ; Xie et al. (2024) ; Koh et al. (2024) . Meanwhile, directly deploying powerful proprietary models for every task remains commercially cost-prohibitive, so practitioners rely on lightweight local models that must adapt and evolve post-deployment. A natural solution to mitigate these deployment-phase errors is online teaching. Under this paradigm, whenever the student encounters an execution failure, the teacher is queried to produce a corrective demonstration, thereby updating the student before the next streaming task arrives Hinton et al. (2015) . Unlike standard online reinforcement learning, where the agent explores freely, here the agent is already deployed and first-pass success matters on every episode. This deployment-time online adaptation setting remains, to our knowledge, under-explored for web agents. The most intuitive implementation to realize this workflow is to pair every student failure with a full teacher trajectory and directly feed both elements into a trajectory-level preference optimization objective such as DPO Rafailov et al. (2024) . Nevertheless, we argue that such an unselective, full-trajectory strategy inherently suffers from inefficient supervision allocation, treating expert supervision as an infinite commodity rather than a strictly bottlenecked, strategic resource. This inefficiency manifests acutely at two distinct granularities, corresponding to the critical yet fundamentally overlooked dimensions of when and what to teach. At the episode level ( when ), the baseline treats all student failures as equally worth querying, ignoring that the teacher itself is unstable on many tasks and will fail to produce a usable corrective trajectory, wasting the query budget without return Zhang and Cho (2016) ; Hoque et al. (2022) . At the trajectory level ( what ), it indiscriminately trains on the entire action history, overlooking that long-horizon web sequences are typically riddled with redundant navigation pauses and non-essential actions Belkhale et al. (2023) . Striking a budget-aware balance across both axes simultaneously remains an open and critical challenge. To address this issue, we present Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming , a budget-aware online adaptation framework that systematically orchestrates when and what to teach. Our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to determine when to query the teacher model. Tactically, we devise a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide what to teach by retaining the most informative turns on both sides. Crucially, both components are fully compatible with various preference optimization objectives, allowing our framework to be seamlessly applied to standard criteria such as DPO Rafailov et al. (2024) and SimPO Meng et al. (2024) . Experiments on MiniWoB Liu et al. (2018) and TimeWarp Ishmam and Marino (2026) show that our method achieves comparable online first-pass success to the full-trajectory baselines while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. The contributions of this paper are: ∙ \bullet We formulate online web-agent teaching as a budget allocation problem along two axes: when to query the teacher and what turns to retain for training. ∙ \bullet We introduce a solvability-aware teacher gate that reduces unnecessary teacher queries based on historical teacher outcomes. ∙ \bullet We introduce a score-guided turn selection that reduces redundant training tokens based on the student’s current log-probability. ∙ \bullet Experiments on two online web-agent benchmarks validate the framework, showing comparable first-pass success with substantially reduced teacher-query and student-training costs. 2 Related Work 2.1 Web Agents and Online Adaptation Online adaptation for web agents differs from standard online reinforcement learning, where the agent explores freely to maximize long-term reward. In our setting the agent is already deployed, first-pass success matters on every episode, and teacher supervision carries real cost. Early web-agent work such as WebGPT Nakano et al. (2021) and WebShop Yao et al. (2022) learns primarily from successful demonstrations. LEAP Choudhury and Sodhi (2025) introduces iterative fine-tuning from privileged AI feedback on student failures, but assumes unrestricted teacher access and optimizes for final model quality rather than first-pass success on each episode as it arrives. Other approaches improve agents through inference-time experience reuse without gradient updates Shinn et al. (2023) ; Zhao et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2023) . On the training side, DPO Rafailov et al. (2024) replaces explicit reward modeling Christiano et al. (2017) ; Schulman et al. (2017) with direct preference optimization, and recent work extends it to trajectory-level, segment-level, or step-level agent objectives Shi et al. (2024) ; Kong et al. (2025) ; Lai et al. (2024) ; Xiong et al. (2024) ; Song et al. (2024) ; Cao et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026b) . These methods focus on how to construct the preference loss from a given trajectory pool. We instead study which trajectories to collect and which turns to retain under budget constraints. 2.2 Active and Budget-Aware Imitation Selectively requesting expert supervision originates from active learning Settles (2009) and active imitation learning, where learners query costly expert interventions only on informative states. DAgger Ross et al. (2011) iteratively queries expert actions on learner-visited states to mitigate compounding errors, but it assumes unrestricted expert access. Subsequent variations reduce this cost by gating queries on safety or novelty signals. For instance, SafeDAgger Zhang and Cho (2016) queries only on predicted deviations, ThriftyDAgger Hoque et al. (2022) targets an explicit intervention budget, and HG-DAgger Kelly et al. (2019) allows human-gated interventions in embodied control. These methods decide whether to query at the level of individual states using local uncertainty signals. In contrast, our teacher gate estimates whether the current failure is teacher-solvable based on historical outcomes. Furthermore, none of these methods address what to retain once a demonstration is collected. While prior work on demonstration quality Belkhale et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2026a) filters entire episodes, we focus on a finer turn-level selection mechanism. 2.3 Difficulty-Aware Data Selection for Preference Learning A separate line of work uses the current model’s own scores as a signal for selecting or weighting training data. Perplexity- and log-probability-based filtering has been used to curate pretraining and fine-tuning corpora by retaining examples the model finds informative Ankner et al. (2025) ; Xie et al. (2023) ; Marion et al. (2023) , and hard-example mining and curriculum strategies have long been used to focus training on instances the current model gets wrong Shrivastava et al. (2016) ; Bengio et al. (2009) . In preference learning, recent work moves from full-response DPO toward finer-grained credit assignment, including step-level Lai et al. (2024) ; Xiong et al. (2024) , segment-level Kong et al. (2025) , and token-level Zeng et al. (2024) objectives that re-weight or restrict the contrastive signal to portions of the response. These approaches share the high-level intuition of concentrating supervision on informative portions, but they typically apply a single criterion uniformly and operate at sub-action granularity. Our turn-level selection differs by operating at the interaction-turn level and applying a dual criterion: hardest turns on the positive side, most-likely-to-repeat turns on the negative side. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation We consider a fixed-order online task stream { x t } t = 1 T \{x_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} Shalev-Shwartz (2025) , where each task x t x_{t} corresponds to a web navigation goal. The student policy π θ \pi_{\theta} processes tasks sequentially in a first-pass manner: at episode t t , the student executes independently and produces trajectory τ t S = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s L , a L ) \tau_{t}^{S}=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{L},a_{L}) , where s i s_{i} denotes the page state and a i a_{i} the student action. If the episode succeeds, the system records the result and continues. If it fails, the system must decide whether to allocate a teacher intervention. The teacher policy π T \pi_{T} (e.g., GPT-4o Hurst et al. (2024) ), when invoked, executes independently on the same task and produces teacher trajectory τ t T \tau_{t}^{T} . If the teacher succeeds, ( τ t T , τ t S ) (\tau_{t}^{T},\ \tau_{t}^{S}) forms a matched positive-negative trajectory pair that can be used to update the student. Let ℛ t ∈ { 0 , 1 } \mathcal{R}_{t}\in\{0,1\} denote whether π θ \pi_{\theta} succeeds on task x t x_{t} at its first attempt. Our objective is to maximize online first-pass success under a teacher-query budget B T B_{T} and a student training-token budget B S B_{S} : max ⁡ ∑ t = 1 T θ ⁡ ℛ t , s.t. ​ N T ≤ B T , N S ≤ B S , \max_{\theta}\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{R}_{t},\quad\text{s.t.}\ N_{T}\leq B_{T},\ N_{S}\leq B_{S}, (1) where N T N_{T} is the total number of teacher queries and N S N_{S} is the total number of student training tokens. 3.2 Method Overview We find that straightforwardly querying the teacher after every student failure and optimizing full trajectories indiscriminately wastes budget at both the episode and turn levels. This inefficiency arises because some failures are inherently unresolvable for the teacher, while even successful rollouts contain redundant, task-specific details with minimal learning value. To resolve these inefficiencies, we organize online teaching into a two-stage mechanism as illustrated in Figure 1 . The solvability-aware teacher gate first operates at the episode level to decide whether a student failure warrants an expert rollout. Subsequently, the score-guided turn selection mechanism functions at the turn level to filter the most informative turns from both the positive and negative trajectories, assembling a trimmed preference pair. This optimized pair is then utilized to update the student via a trajectory-level preference optimization objective. Online teaching is fundamentally a streaming setting: the student receives tasks one by one and must adapt as the stream unfolds. We therefore organize each benchmark into a fixed-order online task stream and use that stream as a controlled evaluation protocol shared across all methods. MiniWoB ( Liu et al., 2018 ) is instantiated as a 125-episode stream covering form filling, email operations, search, and other common web interaction patterns. TimeWarp ( Ishmam and Marino, 2026 ) is instantiated as a 150-episode stream with longer and more heterogeneous tasks, placing greater demands on cross-task generalization. The task ordering is completely fixed offline and reused for every method, so that any difference in observed performance reflects the online learning behavior rather than variation in the task sequence, and all methods report first-pass results on the same evaluation stream of tasks. Baselines. Baseline Student applies no online teaching and reflects the student’s initial capability. Full trimmed pairs with per-turn scores are given in Appendix C . A representative MiniWoB case is use-autocomplete , where the goal is to enter an item beginning with “Gua” and ending with “uam”. The teacher types the prefix to trigger the autocomplete dropdown, picks the suggestion Guam , edits it into Guaguam , and submits. Score-guided selection retains the autocomplete-trigger and the subsequent text edit while dropping the trailing submit, which the student already handles. The matching student-failure trajectory submits the prefix prematurely, retries, and eventually enters the malformed word Guamau . The selector retains exactly these turns, capturing the failure mode the student is most likely to repeat. The trimmed pair thus concentrates the imitation signal on the corrective subroutine and the contrastive signal on the recurring error. The same behavior carries over to longer TimeWarp tasks. On a multi-hop search task that requires opening the fourth result for “Utah”, identifying “New Orleans” as the first city in the article, searching for it, and reporting the final state name from its fourth result, the teacher’s complete trajectory contains routine search-box fills and Go clicks. Selection drops the initial search-box fill and both routine Go clicks, while retaining the two cross-article jumps, the intermediate New Orleans query, and the final answer, which together form the actual reasoning chain the student must learn. The matching student trajectory never reaches this chain: it diverts into the Sci/Tech section and opens an unrelated technology article, and the negative side preserves exactly this divergence while dropping the closing “incomplete task” message. 5 Conclusion In this work, we investigated online teaching for web agents under realistic budget constraints. Driven by the fact that deploying proprietary models is commercially cost-prohibitive, we enabled lightweight local models to effectively adapt and evolve post-deployment. To eliminate the inefficiencies of unresolvable queries and redundant execution turns in full-trajectory optimization, we realized a two-stage budget allocation framework. Specifically, our method integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate using a k-NN historical memory to filter queries alongside a score-guided turn selection mechanism to retain only highly informative execution segments. This joint formulation allows the student model to systematically establish a clear understanding of when to seek external assistance and what critical behaviors to replicate. Experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp show that our framework achieves comparable or superior online success compared to trajectory-level DPO while reducing teacher calls by 22.6% and student training compute by 52.1% on average. These substantial gains establish a highly cost-effective paradigm for future scalable online intelligence. Limitations Our evaluation focuses on simulated web-agent benchmarks. Extending the framework to live websites, multi-modal computer-use tasks, or non-English interfaces is a natural next step but does not require architectural changes. The teacher gate uses a standard text-embedding model for k k -NN retrieval; while this worked well in our setting, environments with highly heterogeneous page structures may benefit from domain-adapted embeddings. The current turn selection criterion is based solely on the student’s log-probability. Incorporating additional signals such as state novelty or action diversity could further refine the selection, though our ablations suggest the current criterion already captures the dominant source of variation. Finally, our framework assumes a single fixed teacher model. Exploring multi-teacher or self-improving teacher configurations is an interesting direction for future work. Appendix A Agent and Prompt Configuration All rollouts use the standard GenericAgent class from AgentLab on top of BrowserGym Chezelles et al. (2025) with the default FLAGS_GPT_4o preset. We did not modify the AgentLab prompt template or action parser. The contributions of this paper are in the teacher query gate, turn scoring and selection, and the student update logic, not in hand-engineered web-agent prompts. Teacher and student agents share the same observation, action, and prompt configuration and differ only in the chat-model backend: the teacher uses the OpenAI API (GPT-4o), and the student uses a local vLLM endpoint serving Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, with rollout log-probability access exposed by the inference wrapper. Observation. The agent observes the page through the AXTree representation provided by BrowserGym, augmented with the currently focused element, the recent interaction history, the recent action history, and current error logs. Visible and clickable tags are preserved in the AXTree. HTML dumps, screenshots, set-of-mark annotations, coordinate extraction, and historical thoughts are disabled. Concretely, the relevant FLAGS_GPT_4o.obs fields are set as: use_ax_tree=True , use_html=False , use_screenshot=False , use_som=False , use_focused_element=True , use_history=True , use_action_history=True , use_think_history=False , use_error_logs=True , extract_visible_tag=True , extract_clickable_tag=True , extract_coords=False . Action Space. We use the standard bid-based high-level action set from BrowserGym ( action_set.subsets=("bid",) ), restricted to single-action steps ( multiaction=False ). The exact set of available actions depends on the environment: MiniWoB tasks typically expose click , fill , and keyboard_press . TimeWarp additionally exposes navigation actions such as go_back , goto , tab_focus , and send_msg_to_user . Action descriptions are kept in their default short form ( long_description=False , individual_examples=False ). Prompt Switches. We use the default FLAGS_GPT_4o prompt switches: use_thinking=True , use_abstract_example=True , use_concrete_example=True , use_hints=True , use_plan=False , use_memory=False , use_criticise=False , enable_chat=False . The prompt token budget is max_prompt_tokens=40000 with up to max_trunc_itr=20 truncation iterations when the budget is exceeded. Appendix B Full Hyperparameter and Gate Configuration This appendix lists training, optimizer, and gate configuration details that are condensed in Section 4 (Implementation details). LoRA and Training Objectives. All methods fine-tune the student with LoRA (rank = 16 =16 , scaling = 32 =32 , dropout = 0.05 =0.05 ) on q_proj , k_proj , v_proj , o_proj , gate_proj , up_proj , and down_proj . Naive SFT applies only an SFT update to an available positive teaching trajectory. DPO uses the standard objective in Eq. 3 with β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 and an explicit reference model; the reference is the current stable student state for each update, with the clean base model used for the first update. SimPO uses the reference-free objective in Eq. 4 with β = 2.0 \beta=2.0 and γ = 0.5 \gamma=0.5 . DPO and SimPO use no SFT preheat, auxiliary SFT loss, or anchor SFT examples. After every successful update, the promoted student state is used for the next episode. Optimizer. We use AdamW with learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} on MiniWoB and 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} on TimeWarp, warmup ratio 0.05 0.05 , effective batch size 8 8 , and 1 1 epoch per online update. Maximum sequence lengths are 4,000 tokens for MiniWoB and 7,000 tokens for TimeWarp. Teacher Gate. The teacher memory retrieves k = 10 k=10 neighbors with similarity bandwidth κ = 0.16 \kappa=0.16 . The solvability threshold λ \lambda and exploration evidence threshold ε exp \varepsilon_{\rm exp} are 0.35 0.35 / 0.50 0.50 on MiniWoB and 0.30 0.30 / 0.50 0.50 on TimeWarp. The semantic task representation ϕ ⁡ ( x ) \phi(x) is computed by encoding the string task=<task_name>; goal=<task_goal> with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small OpenAI (2024) . The embedding API is called once per gate evaluation, and its token cost is negligible compared to the teacher rollout cost and is not counted in the teacher token totals. Turn Selection. Turn budgets are top- 3 3 /side for MiniWoB and top- 4 4 /side for TimeWarp. Negative-side scoring reuses the log-probabilities recorded during the student’s own rollout and incurs no additional cost. Positive-side scoring requires one student forward pass per teacher-positive turn. Appendix D PFLOPs Accounting This appendix details how the Student Total PFLOPs column reported in Section 4 is computed. All numbers are derived from a single accounting pass over the exported per-update datasets, rather than from in-flight runtime estimates. Dense-equivalent assumption. We compute student-side PFLOPs using a dense-transformer equivalent with P = 3 × 10 9 P=3\times 10^{9} parameters, matching the parameter count of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters but the forward and backward passes still involve the full dense weights, so the dense-equivalent count is the appropriate coefficient for compute reporting. Training PFLOPs. Training cost is recomputed from the exported per-update datasets, not from runtime estimates. For each online update, we re-tokenize the dataset files with the student tokenizer under the run’s maximum sequence length. We apply method-specific coefficients reflecting the number of forward and backward passes per training token: • Naive SFT and SimPO : coefficient 6 6 (one forward + one backward pass), Train PFLOPs = 6 ⋅ P ⋅ N train 10 15 . \text{Train PFLOPs}=\frac{6\cdot P\cdot N_{\mathrm{train}}}{10^{15}}. (5) • DPO-based methods : coefficient 8 8 , because DPO requires two forward passes (policy and reference) plus one backward pass per training token, Train PFLOPs = 8 ⋅ P ⋅ N train 10 15 . \text{Train PFLOPs}=\frac{8\cdot P\cdot N_{\mathrm{train}}}{10^{15}}. (6) For methods with score-guided turn selection, the positive-side scoring forward pass (coefficient 2 2 ) is added to the objective-dependent training cost: Student Total PFLOPs = c obj ⋅ P ⋅ N train + 2 ⋅ P ⋅ N score + 10 15 , \text{Student Total PFLOPs}=\frac{c_{\mathrm{obj}}\cdot P\cdot N_{\mathrm{train}}+2\cdot P\cdot N^{+}_{\mathrm{score}}}{10^{15}}, (7) where c obj = 6 c_{\mathrm{obj}}=6 for Naive SFT and SimPO and c obj = 8 c_{\mathrm{obj}}=8 for DPO. Here, N score + N^{+}_{\mathrm{score}} is the token count of the positive-side scoring requests, read from the per-update score request log. For methods without turn selection, Student Total PFLOPs equals Train PFLOPs directly. Per-update Tokens. Each successful online update trains only on the teaching package produced for the current episode. Previously collected teaching packages are not replayed by the main training path. The accounting pass re-tokenizes each exported per-update dataset and counts its tokens once, on the update where they contribute to the gradient. Negative-side Scoring is Excluded. Negative-side turns are generated by the student policy itself during rollout, so the per-turn log-probabilities log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a j S ∣ s j S ) \log\pi_{\theta}(a_{j}^{S}\mid s_{j}^{S}) used by the negative-side selector are available as rollout-time inference outputs and do not require a separate forward pass.
